key_insight: Training vision models with a human-inspired developmental visual diet shifts them from texture-driven to shape-driven perception, producing substantially more robust and generalizable visual inference with lower resource cost.
problem_solved: Addresses the fragility and texture-bias of standard vision models by closing the gap between AI training regimes and human visual development, enabling stronger out-of-distribution and corruption robustness without heavy compute or complex defenses.
method: Design a developmental visual diet and curriculum inspired by human infant visual statistics (e.g., progressive exposure to object-centric, varied-scale, and temporally structured views).
Train standard vision architectures using this developmental diet and compare to conventional ImageNet-style training.
Evaluate models on shape-vs-texture diagnostics and robustness benchmarks (corruptions, OOD tests) to quantify increased shape-bias and improved performance.
impact: Provides a practical, resource-efficient strategy for improving model robustness and generalization by rethinking training data/curriculum rather than model complexity. Practitioners can adopt developmental-diet principles to boost shape-based recognition and OOD resilience in production systems.
visual_elements: Timeline/flow showing developmental visual diet stages (early coarse views → object-centric views → varied contexts).

paper_title: Adopting a human developmental visual diet yields robust and shape-based AI vision
paper_authors: Zejin Lu, Sushrut Thorat, Radoslaw M. Cichy, Tim C. Kietzmann
